description: The Himalayas are the youngest fold mountain range in the world. They were formed by the convergence of the Eurasian Plate and the Indian Plate, which uplifted the sedimentary rocks accumulated in the ancient Tethys Sea.

sections.title: Origin and Geographical Extent
sections.description: A comprehensive overview of the origin, formation, and physical dimensions of the Himalayan mountain system.

key_concepts.explanation: Around 50 million years ago, the northward drift of the Indian Plate caused a massive collision with the Eurasian Plate. This intense compression folded the sediments of the intervening Tethys Sea, giving rise to the Himalayas.

At both extremities (Nanga Parbat in the west and Namcha Barwa in the east), the Himalayan ranges take a sudden, sharp southward turn. This acute geographical feature is known as a hairpin bend or Syntaxial Bend.

important_facts.fact: The Himalayas stretch in a continuous arc shape covering a distance of approximately 2400 km from west to east.
Their width varies significantly, from about 400 km in Kashmir to roughly 150 km in Arunachal Pradesh.

sections.title: The Trans-Himalayas
sections.description: The mountain ranges located immediately to the north of the Great Himalayas, predominantly situated in Tibet (hence also called the Tibetan Himalayas).

geographical_data.key_characteristics: Often referred to as the 'Backbone of High Asia'. It houses India's highest peak, K2 (Godwin Austen - 8611m), and the strategically vital Siachen Glacier.

geographical_data.location_or_origin: Located south of the Karakoram Range
geographical_data.key_characteristics: The Shyok River flows between the Karakoram and Ladakh ranges. Mount Rakaposhi is its highest peak, globally renowned for having the steepest slope.

geographical_data.location_or_origin: Located south of the Ladakh Range
geographical_data.key_characteristics: The Indus River flows in a northwest direction through the deep gorge situated between the Ladakh and Zanskar ranges.

sections.title: Main Himalayan Ranges
sections.description: The latitudinal (longitudinal) division of the Himalayas from north to south into three parallel ranges.

key_concepts.explanation: The northernmost, most continuous, and highest range with an average elevation of 6,000 meters. Iconic peaks like Mount Everest (8848.86m) and Kangchenjunga (8586m) are located here.

Situated south of the Himadri with an average elevation of 3700-4500 meters. The Pir Panjal and Dhauladhar are its most prominent ranges. It is highly famous for hill stations like Shimla, Manali, and Darjeeling.

The outermost and youngest range with an average elevation of 900-1100 meters. The longitudinal valleys lying between the Lesser Himalayas and the Shiwaliks are called 'Duns' in the west (e.g., Dehradun) and 'Duars' in the east (e.g., Haridwar).

important_facts.fact: Mount Everest, the highest peak in the world, is known as 'Sagarmatha' in Nepal and 'Chomolungma' in Tibet.

sections.title: Regional Division of the Himalayas
sections.description: The longitudinal (west to east) division of the Himalayas based on river valley demarcations, originally classified by Sir Sydney Burrard.

geographical_data.location_or_origin: Between the Indus River and the Sutlej River
geographical_data.key_characteristics: Spans 560 km in length. It encompasses major ranges including the Karakoram, Ladakh, Zanskar, and Pir Panjal.

geographical_data.location_or_origin: Between the Sutlej River and the Kali River
geographical_data.key_characteristics: Situated primarily in the state of Uttarakhand. Nanda Devi (7817m) is the highest peak in this regional division.

geographical_data.location_or_origin: Between the Kali River and the Teesta River
geographical_data.key_characteristics: The longest (800 km) and tallest of all divisions. It is home to the mighty peaks of Mount Everest, Lhotse, and Makalu.

geographical_data.location_or_origin: Between the Teesta River and the Dihang (Brahmaputra) River
geographical_data.key_characteristics: Spans 750 km across Sikkim, Assam, and Arunachal Pradesh. Namcha Barwa is the prominent peak here.

sections.title: Important Passes of the Himalayas
sections.description: Natural mountain corridors across the Himalayan ranges that are historically and strategically crucial for trade and transport.

key_associations.extra_info: It is the highest mountain pass in India, providing a vital route connecting Ladakh with the Xinjiang province of China.
Located in the Pir Panjal range, it connects Jammu to Srinagar. The famous Jawahar Tunnel was constructed beneath this pass.
Connects Shimla to Tibet. The mighty Sutlej River enters India from Tibet through this specific pass.
A historically significant branch of the ancient Silk Route. It provides a strategic passage into Tibet via the Chumbi Valley.
Connects the western borders of Arunachal Pradesh with Lhasa, Tibet, navigating through the scenic Tawang Valley.
